claims.text: Rapidly quenched FeCoNiTi has a continuous fcc matrix containing dispersed C14 Laves-phase precipitates.
The C14 Laves phase in FeCoNiTi is enriched in Ti and transition metals.
Ti is nonmagnetic or weakly magnetic in the relevant FeCoNiTi chemical environments.
Ti at the fcc/C14 interface couples antiferromagnetically to Fe, Co, and Ni spins in the fcc phase.
Antiferromagnetic interfacial coupling reduces the effective moment per atom and suppresses the saturation magnetization of the fcc phase.
The Ti-rich interfacial chemical environment further suppresses the already limited orbital moments of the fcc phase.
The C14 phase is a mechanically hard intermetallic phase.
The C14 phase has high magnetocrystalline anisotropy that may be enhanced by Ti electronic structure.
Dispersed C14 particles and fcc/C14 interfaces impede domain-wall motion and thereby increase coercivity.
Rapid quenching likely produces a hierarchical nanoscale distribution of C14 particles and a high density of pinning centers.
Spin fluctuations can modify element-resolved magnetic moments in an fcc high-entropy alloy.
The dual-phase FeCoNiTi alloy should have a saturation magnetization below 80 emu/g and significantly below that of single-phase fcc FeCoNi.
Interfacial pinning and C14-related anisotropy should produce a coercivity of approximately 667 Oe at 400 K.
Single-phase fcc Fe-Co-Ni alloys have coercivity capped at about 100 Oe because of insufficient orbital moments and a lack of pinning centers.
The transitions near 1084 K, 214 K, and 168 K arise from distinct Curie or Néel temperatures of the fcc matrix and coupled fcc/C14 interfacial regions.
Removing the C14 phase or reducing Ti below the level needed for substantial C14 formation should limit the coercivity enhancement.
The coercivity enhancement should diminish above the Curie temperature of the fcc phase or the Néel temperature of the coupled interface.
A spin-polarized DFT comparison of the fcc phase with and without a Ti-containing interface can test whether Ti changes the spin density of states at the Fermi level.
Comparing a dual-phase alloy, a nominally composition-matched single-phase fcc control, and a C14-dominant alloy can help separate phase-specific magnetic behavior.
A single-phase fcc control with coercivity above 400 Oe, a low-coercivity C14-dominant alloy, or no calculated Ti-induced electronic-structure change would falsify specified parts of the mechanism.
